# Set Up Different Alexa+ Routines for Weekday and Weekend Mornings

> **In short:** To get different behavior on weekdays vs weekends, you create two separate Alexa+ routines — one scheduled for Mon–Fri, one for Sat–Sun. Day-of-week is set on the whole routine, not on individual actions, so two routines is the honest way.

Saturday morning, your Echo starts the weekday news flash — and that's the moment most people realize one routine can't quietly branch into "weekday actions" and "weekend actions" inside itself. The supported way is to build two routines and schedule each on the days you want. This guide walks you through both, from opening the Routines screen to testing each one out loud.

## Before you start
- An Amazon account signed in on at least one Echo device, with the Echo powered on and connected to Wi-Fi.
- The **Alexa app** on a phone or tablet (free on iOS and Android), signed in to the same Amazon account as the Echo.
- Two short, easy-to-say names picked out — one for weekdays, one for weekends.
- About **15 minutes** the first time, closer to **5 minutes** once you've done it once.

## Step 1 — Open the Routines section
In the Alexa app, look at the bottom-right corner of the screen for a tab that looks like three horizontal lines or dots (sometimes labeled **More**). Tap it, then look for an option that says something like **Routines**. If you can't find it there, look in a **Settings** or **Automations** area, or use the search bar at the top of the app to type "Routines". When you land on the Routines screen, you'll see a list of any routines you've already created, with a button at the top — often a **+** symbol or a label like **Create Routine** — to start a new one.

If your version of the app puts Routines somewhere else, try the **Settings** tab and look for an **Automations** or **Routines** subsection — Amazon moves this between updates.

💬 Example: routine name — `Weekday Morning`

You'll know it worked when the screen shows a fresh form with fields for a name, a "When this happens" trigger, and an "Add action" button.

## Step 2 — Name the routine and pick the days it runs
Tap the routine name field and type a short phrase you'll remember saying, like `Weekday Morning`. Then look for a "When" or "Schedule" section. If you see an option like "At a specific time," tap it and set the time you want — say, **6:30 AM**. Then look for a day picker, usually a row of seven checkboxes or buttons labeled Mon, Tue, Wed, Thu, Fri, Sat, Sun. Check **Mon through Fri** and leave Sat and Sun unchecked. This day picker is the only place Alexa+ stores weekday vs weekend logic — there is no separate per-action day filter.

If the app shows a **Voice** option instead of typing the trigger phrase, tap the microphone icon and say the phrase out loud; the app will transcribe what it heard so you can confirm the spelling.

💬 Example: name `Weekday Morning`, voice trigger *Alexa, start my weekday morning*, time **6:30 AM**, days **Mon–Fri only**

You'll know it worked when the routine form shows your time, and the days row has Mon through Fri selected, with Sat and Sun greyed out or unchecked.

## Step 3 — Add the weekday actions
Tap the **Add action** button. The app shows categories like Music, Smart Home, Calendar, Weather, and News — pick the one you want for each step. Add the things you only want on weekdays: a news flash, traffic for your commute, the office lights turning on, the coffee maker clicking to life. For each action, follow the prompts to pick the device, playlist, or skill from a list — don't type device names by hand if you can avoid it, because the spelling has to match exactly. When you're done adding weekday actions, save the routine, usually with a **Save** button at the top-right of the screen.

If a particular action asks for its own time or day filter, just leave it at the default — Alexa+ only filters days on the whole routine, not on individual actions inside it.

💬 Example: actions — **News → Flash Briefing**, **Smart Home → Turn on "Kitchen Lights"**, **Smart Home → Turn on "Coffee Maker" plug**

You'll know it worked when the routine screen shows your weekday actions in a list, and the days row at the top still confirms Mon–Fri only.

## Step 4 — Test the weekday routine out loud
With the routine saved, stand near your Echo and say the trigger phrase out loud — for example, "Alexa, start my weekday morning." Listen for the news flash, watch for the lights to come on, and listen for the coffee maker's click. If something doesn't fire, the most common cause is the routine being switched off, or the device name in the action not exactly matching the real device name — go back into the routine and check.

Alexa+ doesn't always offer a dedicated in-app "Test routine" button, so speaking the trigger phrase is usually the fastest way to confirm it works. There is also no way to simulate "today is a Saturday" inside the app — the routine only fires when its schedule says so.

💬 Example: say `Alexa, start my weekday morning` and listen for the news flash within a few seconds.

You'll know it worked when each weekday action runs in the order you set, and your Echo doesn't complain about a missing device or skill.

## Step 5 — Create a separate weekend routine
Go back to the Routines list (the same screen as Step 1) and tap **Create Routine** again. Give it a different name — something like `Weekend Morning` or `Saturday Slow Start` — so you can tell them apart at a glance. Set the time you want (a later hour is fine if you sleep in on weekends). This time, in the days row, check **only Sat and Sun** and leave Mon through Fri unchecked.

You can give the weekend routine a totally different voice phrase, or use the same phrase on both routines — Alexa+ just runs whichever routine is scheduled for today, so there's no clash as long as the day pickers don't overlap.

💬 Example: name `Weekend Morning`, time **8:00 AM**, days **Sat–Sun only**

You'll know it worked when the new routine appears in your list next to the weekday one, and its days row shows only Sat and Sun selected.

## Step 6 — Add the weekend-only actions
In the new weekend routine, tap **Add action** and pick the things you only want on Saturday and Sunday: a sleepy playlist, a slow light fade, no news flash, maybe the coffee maker staying off. Save the routine the same way you did in Step 3. Then double-check that this routine's days row is Sat–Sun only, not every day — otherwise it will also fire on weekdays and fight the other routine for control of your devices.

If both routines happen to share a device (say, the same smart plug), the weekend routine can include its own "off" or "skip" action for that device — Alexa+ will run whichever routine is scheduled for today.

💬 Example: actions — **Music → Play "Slow Morning" playlist**, **Smart Home → Turn off "Bedroom Lights" fade-out**, **Weather → Read forecast** (skip the news flash entirely)

You'll know it worked when the weekend routine shows only the steps you want, and a glance at the days row confirms Sat–Sun only — no overlap with the weekday routine.

## Step 7 — Save and let the calendar do the work
Both routines are now saved. From here on, Alexa+ runs the weekday one Mon–Fri at your chosen time and the weekend one Sat–Sun at its chosen time — you don't have to do anything. The day-of-week picker is the only "branching" Alexa+ offers for routines; there is no per-action day filter, no "if I'm home, do this; if I'm away, do that" logic in the standard routine builder, and no way to make one routine do different things on different days. Two routines scheduled on different days is the supported path.

If a routine suddenly stops firing one morning, the first things to check are: is the routine still enabled (the toggle on the list screen), is the Echo online, and did the trigger phrase get accidentally edited from another device.

💬 Example: on Monday morning, expect the weekday routine; on Saturday, expect the weekend one. If the wrong one fires, open that routine and check the days row.

You'll know it worked when a full week goes by and each morning plays the right music, news, and lights — without you having to remember which day it is.

## Common mistakes
- **Expecting one routine to branch by day inside itself.** Alexa+ applies day-of-week to the whole routine, not to individual actions, so you can't tag a news flash as "Mon–Fri only" inside a routine that also plays weekend music. Fix: build two routines and schedule each on the days you want.
- **Both routines scheduled to fire on the same day.** If both have Mon–Fri checked, Alexa+ runs both at 6:30 and the actions fight each other for control of your devices. Fix: in the days row, leave the weekend routine on Sat–Sun only and the weekday one on Mon–Fri only — no overlap, no clash.
- **A device renamed on the Smart Home screen but not in the routine.** Alexa+ matches device names exactly, so a renamed plug silently stops working. Fix: open the routine, edit the action, and pick the device from the dropdown list again — don't type it by hand.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** one phrase, two very different mornings — news, lights, and coffee on weekdays, a slow playlist and no rush on weekends. You don't have to remember which day it is, because Alexa+ already does.
- **For your business or work:** the same pattern works for any day-of-week split — opening routines for a home-based shop, focus music on weekdays, lights off on Sundays. Two routines with separate schedules is the same trick in a different costume.
- **If you want to go further:** Alexa+ routines can layer a few more things on top of a single routine — a second time trigger, a smart-home device trigger like "when the front door unlocks," and on some plans a location or weather condition. Per-action branching still doesn't exist, but two routines plus a location condition can cover most everyday cases.

## Try it now
Open the Alexa app, find the Routines section, and build just one routine: a name, a single time, and one action — for example, your favorite morning playlist at 7 a.m. every day. Save it, say the trigger phrase out loud, and confirm the music plays. You've now got the smallest working routine — splitting it into weekday and weekend versions is one extra routine away.
